name: firewood
_note: fuel; 2 dry sticks also make a fire by friction

actions.label: cook
log: The fish begins to hiss upon the flat stone warmed by the fire.
The heat curls the fish upon the stone and brings its juices to the surface.
As the fish browns, drops of fat fall into the glowing embers.
The cooked flesh separates readily from the bones and restores some strength.
You eat the warm fish carefully, leaving little but the bones.
Though still hot enough to burn your fingers, the fish provides a welcome meal.
The raw shellfish is tough and briny, and scarcely satisfies your hunger.
You remove the meat from its shell; it tastes chiefly of salt.
A few mouthfuls of chewy shellfish make a very modest repast.

actions.label: cook
log: The shells open with sharp little reports among the embers.
Heat acts upon the shells until they split and release their steam.
A faint hiss is followed by the cracking of shells in the fire.
The heated shellfish proves tender, with the strong flavour of the sea.
Warm and softened by the fire, the shellfish makes a more agreeable meal.
The shells yield their meat readily once cooked, a considerable improvement.
Sour, then sweet. Your mouth goes purple.
You consume a handful of fruit, grateful for even this small provision.
Sharp and sweet. Not much, but something.

name: rock knife
_note: a sharpened stone: sharp like the knife, but everything takes twice as long with it

name: matches
_note: a box of 10 from the shipwreck; light fire uses one

name: water can
_note: stays when the water is gone; 'fill' at a water source you have explored (the spring, the river)

actions.label: fill
log: You submerge the can in the spring until clear water reaches its brim.
Fresh water enters the vessel with a hollow gurgling sound.
The can is filled from the spring and carefully closed against waste.

actions.label: fill
log: You immerse the vessel in the river until no bubbles rise from its mouth.
The stream presses against the can as it fills with running water.
You draw a full can from the river and fasten its lid firmly.

name: water in the can

log: The water has acquired a faint taste of tin, but quenches your thirst.
You take a long and grateful drink from the can.
After drinking, you close the vessel carefully to preserve the remaining water.

_note: up to 4 drinks; refilled from the water can's 'fill'

log: Hard biscuit and salt meat, soaked with sea water. Still food.
You chew a ration slowly, making it last.
The salted meat and softened biscuit are plain fare, but restore your strength.

name: stones
_note: picked up under the cliff; 2 strike sparks for a fire; for the rock knife, the axe, the hoe and the weir

name: logs
_note: better wood than firewood: chopped in the forest with the axe

name: willow twigs
_note: cut by the river; 20 for a fish trap

name: bark strips
_note: cut from the trees in the forest with something sharp; 4 make a rope

name: rope
_note: twisted from bark strips (craft menu, 3 h); climbs the cliff (kept) and makes snares

name: corn
_note: also the seed for the corn field

log: The raw kernels are hard and starchy, requiring patient chewing.
The uncooked corn proves tough, with only a trace of sweetness.
You strip the small kernels from the cob with your teeth.

actions.label: roast
log: You turn an ear of corn among the embers until its kernels begin to burst.
The outer husk blackens, but the grain beneath ripens to a golden colour.
A pleasant sweetness rises from the corn as it roasts over the heat.
The roasted grain is sweet and carries a flavour of woodsmoke.
You eat the hot corn from the cob, taking care not to burn your fingers.
The cooked corn affords a simple but satisfying meal.
The dried fish is firm and salty, demanding considerable effort to chew.
Smoke has lent the preserved fish a strong flavour and a leathery texture.
Though tough, the dried fish proves filling and should travel well.

actions.label: dry
actions.log: You cut two portions of meat into thin strips and hang them on the drying rack.

actions.label: cook
log: Meat on a stick over the fire, dripping into the flames.
The meat browns slowly above the fire, giving off a rich aroma.
You turn the meat carefully until the heat has penetrated it throughout.
Tough strips of dried meat. You chew slowly.
You chew the smoky strips slowly, finding them unexpectedly nourishing.
The freshly roasted meat is rich and hot, its fat running as you eat.
Such a meal is a luxury upon an island where every mouthful must be earned.
You eat slowly. Real meat.
The honey is so sweet that its flavour seems almost overwhelming.
Honey and wax and a dead bee. Sweet.
The rich honey is drawn from the cells until the comb is nearly empty.
